newsitem.title: UK: Irish Voice editor sees new IRA ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Irish Voice editor sees new IRA ceasefire.

text.p: A leading Irish-American said in remarks published on Thursday that the IRA, which killed two policemen this week, was likely to call a new ceasefire to its war against British rule of Northern Ireland.
Nial O'Dowd, publisher of the Irish Voice newspaper, said in an article in the Irish Times that the truce would be called to allow its political wing, Sinn Fein, entry into peace talks.
"Despite the coming roadblocks and the recent horrific murders, the betting should still be on a new ceasefire," said O'Dowd, an influential figure in the Irish-American lobby.

His article forecast that the IRA would restore a 17-month truce it broke in February 1996 because Sinn Fein is determined that it will take part in the talks, from which it is barred because of the guerrilla campaign.

The article was written days after Irish Republican Army gunmen shot dead two police officers in Lurgan in an attack which stunned a province accustomed to a 28-year conflict in which 3,200 people have been killed.

It has further soured the atmosphere in the run-up to a disputed Protestant Orange Order parade from Drumcree church at Portadown next month which politicians and police fear could ignite province-wide communal violence.

Last year police banned the parade then, under pressure from a wave of violent Protestant protest, allowed it to go ahead through a Roman Catholic Irish nationalist suburb of Portadown, triggering days of Catholic rioting.

O'Dowd said the Lurgan killings were proof of a hardline streak in the IRA which does not believe the Belfast peace talks between pro-British Unionists and pro-Irish nationalists will lead to the united Ireland it seeks.
"There is an irrreconcilable element within the IRA that has an utterly jaundiced view of any political negotiations," he said.

"It is too uncomfortable for such people to contemplate the reality of a messy and uncertain political future, rather than the pristine dream of the day the British longboats finally leave Erin's (Ireland's) shores and the (Irish) Tricolour is run up the mast," he wrote.
O'Dowd said "the current Sinn Fein leadership is, above all, possessed of a relentless strategic vision which allows it to plan through crisis and to keep a firm goal in mind.
"It will have been picking up the pieces and moving on in the hours after the Lurgan killings, as it will post-Drumcree in a few weeks."

"Eyes on the Prize" of inclusive talks could be its motto.Its greatest strength is that no one within or outside its organisation can match its relentless pursuit of its goal of making the republican movement relevant politically," he said.
